1.01 Introduction
This document contains the Life Flight Network Flight and Ground Patient Care Guidelines. As guidelines,
they do not represent a standard of care. Every situation is unique. EMS is conducted in a stressful,
dynamic, and constantly changing environment. These guidelines cannot cover every type of injury,
illness, and complicating circumstance which may be encountered.
Situations will arise which are not covered within these guidelines or mitigate their usefulness, so use
them in conjunction with your training, experience, expertise, and always doing the right thing for the
patient. In such instances, you must function within your scope of practice and consider, when time and
circumstances permit, the use of other available resources, including 911 ground and on-line medical
control, to provide care commensurate with the patient’s injury and/or illness.
Available and relevant evidence was incorporated to support these guidelines. Where evidence was
lacking, we relied on best practices, expert advice, and consensus. These guidelines are reviewed on a
regular basis and updated when necessary to reflect advances in the art and science of critical care
transport.
For the State of Washington, these Patient Care Guidelines have been reviewed, approved, and adopted
by Dr. James Nania, Spokane County Medical Program Director. These protocols have also been
reviewed and approved by the Washington State Department of Health, Office of EMS with the exception
of protocols for non-EMS providers and skills and procedures that are outside the approved skills and
procedures for EMS providers. See the WA State approved skills and procedures for certified providers:
https://www.doh.wa.gov/Portals/1/Documents/Pubs/530173.pdf
As the Life Flight Network Medical Director and supervising physician, I approve these Patient Care
Guidelines and authorize their use by all Life Flight Network Flight Nurses, Flight Paramedics, Flight
Respiratory Therapists, Ground Nurses, Ground Paramedics, and Ground EMTs operating within their
scope of practice.
Matthew Conklin, MD
Life Flight Network Medical Director
Effective Date: 2/10/2026

1.04 Scope of Practice
Licensed and/or certified medical personnel providing patient care on behalf of Life Flight Network must
have a thorough knowledge of applicable state scopes of practice. Under no circumstances will patient
care exceed the scope of practice, training, or competency of an individual.
The Oregon Medical Board, Washington State Department of Health, Montana Board of Medical
Examiners, the Idaho EMS Physician Commission, and Hawaii Medical Board are responsible for the
scope of practice of Emergency Medical Service Providers as well as the requirements and duties of
these providers’ supervising physicians (EMS Medical Directors) in their respective state.
To view the complete Scope of Practice, see:
• Oregon Administrative Rule (OAR) 847-035-0030.
• Washington Administrative Code (WAC): 246-976-182
• Administrative Code of Montana (ACM): 24.156.2771
• Idaho EMSPC Scope of Practice 2020-1 Appendix
• Hawaii Revised Statues (HRS) §16-85-59
Each EMS Provider can perform the procedures of each lower-level certification plus those listed in their
certification level.
Registered Nurses (RN) may legally administer any medication or blood product within their scope of
practice and ordered via protocol, standing order, verbal order, or written order. They may also perform
any skill and/or procedure contained within these guidelines. CFRN Montana nurses get a critical care
endorsement which allows them to function as an EMR equivalent.
Paramedics (PM) may legally administer any medication contained within these guidelines provided the
medication is in their state-specific scope of practice and the medication is administered in accordance
with these guidelines. Refer to the table below for further information by state.
• In Washington, paramedics may transport patients with medications infusing if a departmentapproved Medical Program Director (MPD) protocol is in place and providers have completed
department-approved MPD supplementary training on the medication and protocol.
Authorized medications and routes for paramedic personnel are identified in this document.
• In Oregon and Idaho, paramedics may administer any medication not contained in these
guidelines only when they receive an order from a physician, the medication is legally within
their scope of practice, additional training has been provided as approved by LFN’s Medical
Directors, and where the additional training is documented in the employee’s education
record. In the case of uncommon medications for which the paramedic has no training, the
Flight Nurse will be responsible for the administration and infusions.
Respiratory Therapists in Washington may provide treatment as defined by Scope of Practice
regulations (RCW 18.89.040). The interpretation of these regulations by the Executive Director of
Respiratory Therapists for respiratory care practitioner’s limits medication administration to agents
related to respiratory care.
Surgical cricothyrotomies and chest tubes are not in scope of practice, but our interpretation is needle
thoracostomies and placement of intraosseous lines are in scope, provided additional training has been
provided as approved by LFN’s Medical Directors and where the additional training is documented in the
employee’s education record. Intraosseous lines are not in the scope of practice in Oregon.

2 General Treatments

2.01 Basic Approach to All Patient Contacts
SAFETY IS OUR #1 PRIORITY! IT WILL TAKE PRECEDENCE OVER ALL OTHER CONCERNS!
1. All care shall be performed per these PCGs, except in rare cases where the situation precludes
adherence.
a. Any care not delineated by these PCGs requires documentation of medical decision making to
support provider decisions and care
b. These guidelines serve as a starting point for all patient care. Sound judgement and the best
interests of the patient should always prevail
2. Air medical transport provides speed of transport and improved patient access to any necessary
advanced procedures. Ensure you and your team are At The Ready to provide these services.
Lifesaving interventions delivered too late do not improve survival.
3. Time at the base is time on shift at the service to our communities. In the absence of patient calls
and following the completion of essential daily duties, you must prioritize sleep / rest until confident
you will be able to complete the remainder of your shift with sequential calls.
4. Patients with a Time Sensitive Emergency, whether trauma, stroke, acute coronary syndrome,
pediatric emergency, or other, benefit from resources at a tertiary care facility. After brief initial
stabilization care, you shall expedite air transport. No patient is too unstable for air transport.
a. The assumption is the patient will otherwise succumb to their injuries or illness without
transport
b. In the case of a STEMI with arrest, if a mechanical CPR device is not available, a shorter
duration of suboptimal CPR is preferred to a longer duration of optimal CPR as CPR alone is
not indefinitely sustaining. The goal is rapid delivery to a center which can address or reverse
the cause of the condition
c. See destination determination for further information
5. Use personal protective equipment (PPE) for patient care. An N95 mask is required when caring for
any patient with pneumonia, meningitis, tuberculosis, fever, shortness of breath of unknown etiology,
or sepsis. Patients under investigation (PUI) for COVID-19 require full PPE.
6. End tidal CO2 (ETCO2) is required to be continuously monitored in the following patients:
a. All patients with an advanced airway
b. Patients with respiratory compromise, altered level of consciousness, and/or those receiving
sedatives and/or narcotics
c. All patients receiving ketamine regardless of dose or indication
7. Advanced airway transfers: disconnect ventilator/BVETT if tolerated; verify ETT/SGA securement in
commercial holder prior to movement; confirm placement with ETCO₂ immediately after each
transfer to prevent risk of unintended extubation.
8. When practical and possible, obtain written consent from the patient before initiating any procedure,
including the administration of blood products.

9. When it is known that the transport will require handoff to a second LFN crew, obtain written orders
for any medications and treatment parameters from the sending provider, when practicable and
possible.
10. The Handtevy resuscitation system is the approved reference for pediatric resuscitation. A lengthbased resuscitation tape may be utilized for pediatric weight estimation.
11. Pediatric medication dosages should not exceed maximum single or total adult dose.
12. Pediatric patients are defined by CAMTS as < 18 years old. However, most patients with any evidence
of secondary sexual characteristics (pubic, axillary, facial hair, and/or breast development) may be
treated per adult guidelines.
a. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, fentanyl, and midazolam infusions should be weight
based for all pediatric patients regardless of weight.
b. Pediatric IV push doses of epinephrine should be dosed AND documented in mL/kg.
c. If transferring a patient to a pediatric ICU, make every effort to contact the receiving physician
prior to transport
13. Pediatric equipment formulas (*with an appropriately sized ETT):
a. ETT size: (Age + 16) / 4
i. Subtract 0.5 for cuffed ETT
b. NG/OG/Foley size: 2x ETT* size
c. ETT Depth: 3x ETT* size
d. Chest tube: 4x ETT* size
14. Pediatric Fluid Guidelines
a. Use D5NS for maintenance fluids
i. If D5 ½ NS is already initiated, switch to D5NS.
b. NS or LR may be used if glucose is contraindicated (head injury, diabetes/hyperglycemia), or if
D5NS is unavailable
c. For infants ≤ 28 days old, D10 may be used as an alternative to D5NS (rather than NS) for
maintenance fluids.
i. LR is contraindicated in this patient population
d. Do NOT give dextrose-containing solutions as a bolus, except when treating hypoglycemia
according to the appropriate guideline.
e. Pediatric maintenance fluid rate formulas:
i. <10 kg : 4 mL/kg
ii. 10 – 20 kg : 40 mL + 2 mL/kg for every kg > 10
iii. >20 kg body weight: 60 + 1 mL/kg for every kg > 20 kg
15. All patients presenting with neurological symptoms (e.g., CVA, AMS, seizure, etc.) should have
ongoing neurological assessment performed and documented at least q 15 minutes.
16. Whether a scene call or interfacility transfer, appropriate primary medical equipment should be taken
from the aircraft to the patient’s location. Consider your environment, as not all situations require all
equipment.

Basic Approach To
All Patient Contacts
17. All medical crew members will have a thorough knowledge of each medication in our formulary.
Providers may decrease the dosage or prolong the administration intervals of any medication with
sedative properties when doing so would decrease adverse effects and still likely obtain the clinical
goal.
a. When administering medications at doses that are outside of this guideline, you must
document your reasoning along with a physical assessment that is related to pain and/or
sedation with pain and/or RASS scores.
18. During handoffs at sending and receiving facilities, coordinate changing of infusions between pumps
to minimize interruptions of any critical infusions.
a. To minimize bedside time during STEMI transfers, heparin, and nitroglycerin infusions may be
clamped and pumps restarted after loading/lifting
19. It is expected that clinicians are familiar with the skills needed to perform advanced procedures.
Regardless of who actually performs the procedure, the second crew member is expected to assist
whenever feasible.
20. Start a large bore IV with LR or saline lock as appropriate. For vasoactive medications, central lines
are preferable, but a good patent peripheral IV is acceptable.
a. Document IV site assessment with vasoactive medications q 15 minutes
b. Consider placing an IO, if vascular access is in question
i. The risk of ischemic necrosis secondary to extravasation is the same, regardless of
which vasoactive medication is utilized
c. Any If necessary and appropriate, any medication or fluid suitable for IV administration,
including blood, may be administered via an IO
21. All syringes containing medications which are not immediately administered (such as push dose
epinephrine) will be labeled with the medication name and concentration.
a. Only draw up the amount of medication you intend to administer into your syringe.
22. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) goals most patients should be a normal SBP, with a few exceptions
which are listed below. Patients being outside of the targeted range may not require immediate
treatment but should be continuously monitored by the crew (i.e., a vasopressor may not be required
before trialing fluid boluses).
a. Normal SBP:
i. Adults: ranges from 90 – 120 mmHg
ii. Children < 10 years old: > 90 + (age x2) mmHg
b. Hypotensive patients:
i. Adults and children: SBP > 90 mmHg
c. Hemorrhagic Shock
i. Adults and children ≥ 10 years: SBP 80 – 90 mmHg or presence of a radial pulse
ii. Children < 10 years: SBP > 80 mmHg or presence of a brachial pulse
d. Evidence of head injury:
i. Adults and children ≥ 10 years: SBP 110 mmHg
ii. Children < 10 years: SBP > 90 + (age x2) mmHg
23. Vital Sign Requirements:
a. Vital signs are required to be transmitted from the monitor to the ePCR via the cloud

Basic Approach To
All Patient Contacts
b. Obtain and document baseline vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO2,ETCO2) and GCS on all patients.
i. Include baseline and ongoing ETCO2 for patients with any managed airway
c. Non-intubated patients: ETCO2 NC documentation is required for patients receiving multiple
doses of pain medications, any amount of ketamine, and those receiving analgesia infusions
or use of sedatives.
d. Q 5 min vitals (or more often as required) for scene calls or unstable transports. The term
“unstable "includes but is not limited to patients:
i. Requiring vasoactive medications (e.g., vasopressor(s), nitroglycerin, nicardipine,
etc…) blood products, and/or multiple fluid boluses for hemodynamic support.
ii. Performance of advanced procedures until vital signs stabilize.
e. Q 15 min vitals for stable transports
f. Q 30 min vitals for extended transports with a stable patient
24. Ventilator Documentation:
a. Ventilator settings and ongoing monitor data is required to be documented q 15 minutes
i. Q 30-minute checks are acceptable for stable transports that exceed 90 minutes and
when the patient’s oxygenation, ventilation, and hemodynamics are stable and
require minimal interventions or adjustments
b. Required documentation elements include:
i. Mode, Rate, VT or target VT, PIP, PEEP, & FiO2
ii. Exhaled tidal volume (VTe)
iii. Cstat (if used to obtain plateau pressure)
iv. Plateau pressure (if applicable)
• If Pplat ≤ 30, only one plateau pressure is required
• If Pplat > 30, document q 15 minutes or until ≤ 30
v.
At least one ETT cuff pressure measurement is required
25. If you are transporting a patient with an existing arterial line or PA catheter, you should continue to
transduce and document the values in your ePCR.

2.02 Basic Approach for BLS Transport Teams
ADULT & PEDIATRIC:
1. If indicated, maintain an open airway through the use of:
• NPA/OPA
• Pharyngeal suctioning device
2. Maintain existing CPAP using a Flow-Safe II if patient is stable and current CPAP/PEEP
level is attainable with Flow-Safe II (usually ≤ 10 cmH2O)
3. Perform tracheobronchial tube suctioning PRN to maintain patency if patient has
tracheostomy tube
BLS
4. Transport stable patients with saline locks, urinary catheters, or in-dwelling vascular
devices as needed
5. Provide care for suspected shock
• Provide hemorrhage control
• Place patient supine
• Do not place in Trendelenburg position
6. Provide care for musculoskeletal injuries as needed
7. Assist an Advanced EMT, EMT-Intermediate, or Paramedic by:
• Assembling and priming IV fluid administration sets
• Opening, assembling, and uncapping preloaded medication syringes and vials
8. Assist a patient with administration of sublingual nitroglycerin and with metered dose
inhalers that have been previously prescribed by that patient’s personal physician and
are in the possession of the patient at the time the EMT is summoned to assist that
patient.
9. For patients requiring minimal control for patient or staff safety, place soft restraints as
needed if patient cannot be verbally calmed or redirected.
• Check and document circulation, motor, and sensation (CMS) initially and q 15
minutes on patients in restraints
• Violent patients require ALS transport
• If patient is placed in soft restraints, complete a QM report

DO NOT LOAD A COMBATIVE PATIENT INTO AN AIRCRAFT OR AMBULANCE unless the
situation is able to be mitigated and controlled by available personnel.
o Dangerous agitation in patients during transport poses significant risks to both the crew
and patient, utilize mitigation techniques prior to loading (e.g., de-escalation,
physical/chemical restraint)
o Agitation can lead to unpredictable and violet behaviors which can compromise safety,
interfere with medical care, and/or destabilize the aircraft
Medical responses involving behavioral emergencies and combative patients are some of the
most perilous emergencies EMS personnel will encounter
o Many of these patients have multiple underlying pathologies, which can be exacerbated by
or derived from illicit substance abuse
o Despite these many challenges, patient care shall be driven by appropriate clinical care,
never at the convenience of law enforcement, and should be focused on
preventing/mitigating hyperthermia, agitated delirium, positional asphyxia, hypoxia, and
physical self-harm.
Consent MUST be obtained for transport7
• Assess for medical causes of altered LOC/violent behavior
o Obtain a blood glucose level and baseline set of vital signs, if able to safely
• For actively agitated patients, provide oxygen as soon as possible consider blow-by for
non-compliant patients.
• Minimize noxious stimuli and create a low stimulus environment as feasible
• Involve law enforcement as early as possible for combative/violent patients requiring
restraint or sedation
• Restraints may be used for patient and/or clinician safety when clinically appropriate
o Do not restrain any patient in the prone position
o ETCO2 and SpO2 must be continuously monitored; distal circulation, motor
function, and sensation must be assessed and documented at least q 15 minutes
o Observe and prevent positional asphyxia, and monitor the airway and respirations
closely
o Any patient restrained with a device provided by law enforcement must have a
LEO ride with the patient that can remove the device if needed
o If restrained, do not release restraints until at the hospital (unless required for
essential patient care)
o Do not leave the patient unattended
o Allow for adequate heat dissipation

6. Assessment Considerations:
a. Among the most difficult tasks in providing care during an adult behavioral
emergency is determining the etiologies of combative patients and treating
accordingly, be it medical, toxicological, or traumatic in nature.
b. Approximately two-thirds of behavioral emergency patients have a non-psychiatric
(organic) etiology:
i. Psychiatric (functional)
ii. Non-psychiatric (organic)
iii. Medical (CVA, hypoglycemia, increased ICP, meningitis, etc.)
iv. Toxicological
7. Consent may be obtained via:
a. Informed consent through discussion with the patient / family
b. Implied consent due to severe injuries or patient inability to demonstrate capacity for
medical decision making
c. Physician consent
d. Law Enforcement does not provide consent for procedures but can request
assistance with maintaining safety of patients in their custody.
8. If the patient has previously been sedated by sending providers, they may potentially lack
capacity for refusal of medical transport
a. You may need to rely on statements of consent given to providers prior to your arrival
b. Consider contacting medical control
9. While rare, droperidol may cause dystonic symptoms, which is treated with diphenhydramine
a. Refer to diphenhydramine formulary entry for dosing

intermittent, repetitive, patterned, tremulous, or jerky movements affecting the
extremities, face, neck, trunk, pelvis, or larynx.

2.05 General Respiratory Care
BLS
1. Supplemental oxygen – apply if needed to keep SpO2:
a. Most patients: > 94%
b. Trauma patients at risk for ischemic injuries or hemorrhagic shock - SpO2 > 95%
c. Burn patients should have supplemental oxygen applied due to risk of inaccurate SpO2
readings
d. Some patients with special needs may require a lower level of O2 saturation, such as COPD
e. Cardiac patients should be treated with oxygen only to maintain SpO2 > 90% (92% - 98%
post ROSC)
ALS & CCT
1. Continuous waveform capnography shall be monitored on all patients with an advanced airway in
place.
2. Monitor capnography via ETCO2 NC for all non-intubated patients with respiratory
compromise, with an altered level of consciousness, and those receiving sedation, narcotics, or
any combination of sedative medications and narcotics.
3. Initiate Rapid Sequence Induction when appropriate
a. The RSI checklist is required to be utilized for all intubations unless a crash airway
b. A bougie should be used as a stylet, especially for anterior airways
i. Adult bougie: ETT size ≥ 5.5 , noting the 5.5 is a tight fit
ii. Pediatric bougie: ETT size ≥3.5, noting the 3.5 is a tight fit
c. A stylet is required for ETTs ≤ 4.0 in patients where a Mac 3 or Mac 4 blade would be
appropriate.
d. The C-MAC should be used beginning with the first intubation attempt
4. All patients with an advanced airway must be placed on and transported via mechanical
ventilator, regardless of estimated transport time. This includes IFTs and scenes calls.
a. Transporting a patient with an advanced airway without use of the ventilator should be
reserved for equipment failure or other rare extenuating circumstances. This may include
excessive leaks with a supraglottic airway device that cannot be adequately addressed.
b. The reason for not utilizing the ventilator must be appropriately documented.
5. The ventilator should be taken into the sending facility when transporting a patient that is intubated
or receiving non-invasive ventilation,
a. Regardless of the patient’s reported respiratory status, the ventilator should always be
taken from the airport or other remote landing locations to the hospital, as patient
conditions frequently change.
b. When changing patients over to LFN’s ventilator, minimize time off the ventilator, without
PEEP, to prevent loss of recruitment.
6. In COVID-19, ARDS and similar pathology, higher ventilator rates/pressures and 100% FiO2 can
potentially harm lung tissue and cause O2 utilization beyond that available for completion of
transport; SpO2 can be maintained ≥ 87% if necessary.

3. Background Information
• Most of the areas served by LFN use one of two LVADs.
o Heartmate II or HeartWare
• The main difference between the two is how they connect to the left ventricle.
o Blood flows via the normal path through the heart until it reaches the left
ventricle.
o The implanted LVAD has a cannula or pump placed in the apex of the heart which
drains blood from the left ventricle into the system pump.
o The pump then drives the blood into the ascending aorta.
o The driveline exits the abdominal wall and connects the internal pump to the
external controller.
o The controller is the brains of the device and controls the power to the pump,
manages the pump speed, and reports alarms and other operating parameters to
the user.
• The controller is connected to an electrical source.
o Two batteries or an AC power unit.
• LVAD patients are typically on anticoagulation medications and complications usually
result from anticoagulation (GI or intracranial bleeds) or pump thrombus (CVAs or pump
thrombosis).

6. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is a disorder due to a specific type of problem with the

electrical pathway potentially leading to unstable ventricular arrhythmias
b. The classic ECG pattern of preexcitation in sinus rhythm is characterized by a
fusion between conduction via the accessory pathway and the normal AV
node/His-Purkinje system
i. The PR interval is short (less than 0.12 seconds) due to rapid AV
conduction through the accessory pathway and bypass of the AV nod
ii. The QRS complex consists of fusion between early and direct ventricular
myocardial activation caused by preexcitation and the later ventricular
activation resulting from transmission through the AV node and the
infranodal conduction system to the ventricles
iii. While beginning earlier than expected, the initial part of ventricular
activation is slow, and the upstroke of the QRS complex is slurred because
of slow muscle-fiber-to-muscle-fiber conduction.

1. About 75% of patients will experience symptoms within one hour, and 90% within 12

2. Type I decompression sickness (mild): typically affects the musculoskeletal, cutaneous,

1. Indicators of worse prognosis (death or permanent neurologic impairment)
a. Duration of submersion >5 minutes (most critical factor)
b. Time to effective basic life support >10 minutes.
c. Resuscitation duration >25 minutes (provided body temperature is >34°C)
d. Age >14 years
e. Glasgow coma score <5
f. Persistent apnea and requirement of cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the
emergency department.
g. Arterial blood pH <7.1 upon presentation
2. Hypothermia may be protective in drowning, however, unless the water is extremely cold
(<5°C/41°F), cooling is usually not rapid enough to provide cerebral protection.
a. Cold water between 5° – 20°C (40 – 68°F) may provide some hypothermic
protection if the patient was seen on the surface for a prolonged period prior to
submersion or a car into the water with question of an air pocket, etc.
b. The important consideration is the patient may have become cold and then dead
(better potential) vs. dead and then cold (poor potential).
3. Any patient resuscitated from drowning or presenting with respiratory symptoms after
submersion (cough, shortness of breath, hypoxia) should be transported.
a. In these patients, there is potential for delayed development of ARDS/noncardiogenic pulmonary edema leading to increased respiratory distress and/or
death over ensuing hours to days (previously called secondary drowning, although
this term is no longer used).
4. Definitions:
a. Drowning: submersion, leading to death within 24-hours.
b. Near downing: submersion with loss of consciousness and survival for at least 24hours.
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE

PEARLS
Drowning
5. Hypoxemia is the most life-threating consequence of near drowning for both salt and
fresh water.
a. Fresh water alters the composition of pulmonary surfactant in the alveoli,
changing their surface tension and leading to alveolar collapse.
b. Saltwater causes protein-rich fluid to extravasate into the alveoli, causing
surfactant to wash out.
c. Both types of water end with V/Q mismatch, intrapulmonary shunting, and
decrease compliance.
6. A key clinical pitfall in the management of the drowning patient is to suction the foam
that comes up from the lungs into the oral cavity during resuscitation.
a. This is often intuitive as we typically suction blood, emesis, or anything else that
could potentially hinder oxygen exchange.
b. Foam in drowning is a result of lung surfactant mixed with water that bubbles up
like soap and water.
c. It is non-toxic and contains lung surfactant that patients’ lungs need.
d. As such it should not be suctioned, as such attempts will delay definitive airway
management.
e. Rather, positive pressure ventilation should be used to push the foam back down
into the lungs.
f. Foam in the upper airway is an indication for endotracheal intubation.
7. As soiling the airway with emesis is common in drowning, the resuscitation team should
be prepared to perform suction assisted laryngoscopy airway decontamination (SALAD).
a. This technique is used to prevent airway soiling during laryngoscopy as a result of
aspirated emesis.
b. SALAD involves using a rigid suction catheter as a sort of tongue depressor to
allow the laryngoscope blade to be placed in the ideal position
c. The suction catheter is then used to decontaminate the proximal esophagus and
stays pinned in the left corner of the patient’s oral cavity.
d. Antiemetics, which may prevent soiling of the airway from emesis, are reasonable
to administer during the resuscitation of the drowning patient.

b. Deep:

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Pain control is an important modifier of both HR and BP and should be addressed early.
2. Monitor urine output and patient mentation to assess perfusion. Assess variation in
blood pressure and heart rate in all extremities (right vs left / upper vs lower).
3. Any mismatch noticed may help to gauge progression of the disease.
4. It is imperative to ensure that you will have enough medication to last the entire
transport.
5. Aortic injury (trauma) and aortic dissection (medical) are different entities, but treatment
of associated tachycardia and hypertension is the same.
6. With traumatic aortic injury, blood is usually contained in a mediastinal hematoma, as a
free rupture is normally fatal within minutes without surgical intervention.
a. Therefore, tachycardia and persistent or recurrent hypotension, especially in the
absence of medical treatment (e.g., esmolol, nicardipine), is usually due to blood
loss from an alternative site.
b. Treat as needed with fluids and/or blood, see Blood Product Administration.
7. Impulse therapy recognizes the damage to the artery from both the pressure as well as
the rate of pulsation.
a. Vasodilators can cause reflex tachycardia. Therefore, the guidance is to start with
a beta blocker and then give further vasodilator, such as nicardipine to achieve
goal blood pressure.

patients with nicardipine and/or labetalol.

1. Nuchal cord describes an umbilical cord that passes 360 degrees around the fetal neck.
2. Breech presentation, which occurs in approximately 3 percent of fetuses at term, describes
the fetus whose presenting part is the buttocks and/or feet.
a. Frank breech – Both hips are flexed and both knees are extended so that the feet are
adjacent to the head (figure 1); accounts for 50 to 70 percent of breech fetuses at
term.
b. Complete breech – Both hips and both knees are flexed (figure 2); accounts for 5 to 10
percent of breech fetuses at term.
c. Incomplete breech presentation - One or both hips are not completely flexed (figure
3); accounts for 10 to 40 percent of breech fetuses at term.
3. Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when, after delivery of the fetal head, further expulsion of
the infant is prevented by impaction of the fetal shoulders within the maternal pelvis.
a. It is an obstetric emergency; thus, the obstetric provider must be able to recognize a
shoulder dystocia immediately and proceed through an orderly sequence of steps to
accomplish delivery in a timely manner.
b. The goal is to prevent fetal asphyxia, permanent Erb's palsy, or death, while also
avoiding physical injury (e.g., fetal fracture, maternal tissue trauma), but the latter is
acceptable if needed to prevent permanent injury of the child.
4. Vertex presentations is when the head of the fetus most commonly faces to the right and
slightly to the rear.
a. This position is said to be the most usual one because the fetus is thus best
accommodated to the shape of the uterus.
5. Uterine inversion occurs when the uterine fundus collapses into the endometrial cavity,
turning the uterus partially or completely inside out.
a. Although a rare complication of vaginal or cesarean birth, it is a life-threatening
obstetric emergency because, if not promptly recognized and treated, uterine
inversion can lead to severe hemorrhage and shock, resulting in maternal death.

1. Signs of increased intracranial pressure/herniation:
a. In patients with an initial GCS ≤ 8, a decrease in the GCS of more than two points.
b. A unilateral, dilated pupil is the hallmark sign of herniation. Progresses to bilateral and
fixed as herniation worsens
c. Decerebrate/extensor posturing
d. Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations/apnea)
e. Hemiparesis on side opposite the dilated pupil
2. The ETCO2 goal for all patients with known or suspected head injuries, including those with
suspected herniation is 35 – 40 mmHg.
a. Hyperventilation to obtain lower ETCO2 goals has not been shown to improve patient
outcomes.
3. Goal serum sodium is 144 – 155 mEq/L. If serum sodium is known and is ≥ 155 mEq/L, avoid
repeat hypertonic saline infusion unless all other options have failed to control herniation
(hyperventilation, 30° elevation of HOB, addition of mannitol if available)
4. Because hypotension associated with traumatic head injuries worsens outcome, no treatment
is typically recommended for hypertension in patients with traumatic hemorrhages. However,
in practice, many neurosurgeons recommend controlling hypertension to an SBP of 140.
a. Ask the sending provider or contact the receiving neurosurgeon to ascertain target BP
b. If BP control is requested, treat per Atraumatic Hemorrhagic Stroke and Cerebral
Edema
5. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), the difference between the MAP and the ICP (CPP = MAP
– ICP), is a useful surrogate. Episodes of hypotension (low MAP), raised ICP, and/or low CPP
are associated with secondary brain injury and worse clinical outcomes
a. CPP goals:
i. Adults: 60 – 70 mmHg
ii. 6 – 17 years: 50 – 60 mmHg
iii. ≤ 5 years: 40 – 50 mmHg
6. Hypotension secondary to penetrating head trauma is usually due to medullary failure and
not hemorrhage.
a. Do not treat with blood unless there is obvious hemorrhage.

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Pathophysiology:
a. Pooling of blood in lower extremities causes a decrease in the amount of blood
circulating to the vital organs
b. Factors worsening suspension trauma include inability to move legs, fatigue,
associated injuries, dehydration, hypothermia, and underlying cardiopulmonary
disease
c. Suspension trauma by itself or subsequent reperfusion of the lower extremities
may lead to loss of consciousness, renal failure, pulmonary embolus, or cardiac
arrest
2. Theories as to cause of death:
a. Blood pooled in the legs lacks oxygen and upon returning to the heart causes
ischemic heart failure
b. On horizontal positioning, a large volume of blood returns to the heart and
overloads the right ventricle
c. Reperfusion injury of the vital organs that became hypoxic during vertical
immobility
d. Injury caused by toxins that accumulated in the blood stored in the legs (similar to
crush injury)
3. Recognize some authorities suggest positioning patient in a sitting position for at least 30
min before horizontal positioning in order to prevent reperfusion injuries. Others
recommend immediate supine positioning, particularly when there are other injuries.
There is no consensus opinion regarding this issue.
a. You may encounter resistance from EMS first responders or bystanders when
attempting to immobilize or treat the patient in a supine position.

• Indications

Any rhythm with a pulse
PEA
Asystole

2. With minimal CPR interruption, place a second set of pads, ensuring there is no overlap
or contact with the other set
a. If there is overlap of pads there is a significant risk of damaging the defibrillators.

8.07 Endotracheal Tube Exchange
• PEARLS
ALS
• Indications
Damaged or uncuffed ETT causing a significant
air leak
ETT placement depth is incorrect causing
ventilation and/or oxygenation issues
• Contraindications
ETT migration that can be corrected by less
invasive means
Inadequate ETT cuff inflation that can be
corrected by increasing the cuff pressure
Equipment:
• All equipment and medications required for intubation
• Bougie
Procedure:
1. Delineate roles for the procedure:
a. Operator will be the crew member performing the tube exchange.
b. Assistant will be the crew member assisting the operator with the exchange.
2. Initiate pre-oxygenation by increasing FiO2 to 100% and place a NC @ 15 LPM.
3. Additional sedation and paralytic agents should be administered.
a. See Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI)
4. Move the patient as needed to optimize operator position, lighting, and patient safety
5. Hold the ETT and have the assistant remove the device or tape securing the ETT
6. Have the assistant advance the bougie into the existing endotracheal tube and advance gently
until the markings that indicate the catheter is properly positioned mid trachea.
7. Stop advancement if hold up is encountered and avoid advancing the bougie deeper than midtrachea
8. The bougie must be maintained in this position for the duration of the procedure
9. Perform laryngoscopy with the video laryngoscope and identify the original tube with the bougie
inserted in the glottic opening
10. Asses the surrounding structure and anatomy for any abnormalities that may impede the
procedure.
11. Maintain the view of the glottic opening throughout the procedure until the new tube is in place
12. Deflate the cuff
13. While the assistant maintains control and position of the bougie, the operator carefully
withdraws the ETT under direct vision until the tip clears the mouth.
14. Once the ETT tip is clear, the operator takes and maintains control and position of the bougie.
15. The assistant carefully removes the ETT over the bougie.
16. The assistant loads the new ETT onto the bougie and carefully advances until the tip of the ETT
reaches the patients mouth and the bougie extends from the proximal end of the ETT.
17. The assistant takes and maintains control and position of the bougie exiting the ETT while the
operator takes and maintains control of the ETT and continues to advance it
18. While maintaining laryngoscopic view, the tube is advanced into the trachea over the bougie
using a 90-degree counter-clockwise to prevent its beveled point from getting caught in the
arytenoid cartilage
19. Inflate the ETT cuff, carefully remove the bougie, verify placement and secure the ETT..
ADULT & PEDIATRIC:
1. ETT exchange is an airway procedure, which risks injury or loss of airway
2. The ETT exchange procedure must always be performed with visualization of the glottic opening
and must NEVER be performed blind
3. To make ETT exchange safe we want to make this procedure as similar as possible to standard
intubation procedures
a. If we are following similar approaches compared to most intubations, when things go
sideways, we can apply the usual principles of airway management

8.11 Hemostatic Agents
PEARLS
BLS
• Indications
Bleeding that cannot be controlled via other
less invasive means.
Contraindications
1. Open the package and remove gauze. Retain the packaging.
2. Remove any saturated gauze from the wound so that the hemostatic agent can directly
contact the bleeding vessels.
3. Pack rolled gauze into wound and use it to apply pressure directly on the bleeding
source.
4. Continue to apply direct pressure for 3 minutes.
5. If the dressing is fully red, then it must be removed and replaced with a new hemostatic
dressing.
a. The previous dressing may not have been applied directly to the bleeding source,
or adequate pressure may not have been held long enough.
6. Once bleeding is controlled, wrap, and tie the bandage to maintain pressure.
a. Attach the product packaging to the patient for transport with them to the
hospital.
7. Do not lift the dressing! “If you peek, you leak.”
ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Hemostatic agents are not exclusively for major hemorrhage. They can also be used to
effectively control “nuisance bleeding” such as head lacerations etc.
2. Dressings can remain in a wound for up to 24 hours.
3. QuickClot dressings are impregnated with an inorganic mineral agent Kaolin and do not
contain any human, animal, or shellfish product, or cause an exothermic reaction.

• Indications
Medication administration when IV access is

• Contraindications

Epistaxis

BLS
Equipment:
1. Mucosal atomizer device (MAD)
2. Small volume syringe (1 – 3 mL)
3. Desired medication
Procedure:
1. Patient should be in a recumbent with head tilted back or supine.
2. Draw up medication into a 1 mL or 3 mL syringe.
a. An extra 0.1 mL of medication should be drawn into the syringe to account for

administration.

1. To improve success, minimize the drug volume and maximize concentration.
a. Ages ≥ 10 years: no more than 1 mL per nostril.
b. Pediatric (< 10 years of age): no more than 0.5 mL per nostril.

Midazolam, and Naloxone

• Indications
Unconscious patient with respiratory
compromise and an absent gag reflex
• Contraindications
Responsive patient with gag reflex
Known esophageal disease
Caustic ingestions
BLS
EQUIPMENT:
• King Airway and syringe of the appropriate size (see below)
• Airway securing device
• Suction
PROCEDURE:
1. Prepare suction and have it readily available
2. Select the correct size KING LT(S)-D based on the patient’s weight or height
3. Test the cuff inflation
4. Pre-oxygenate the patient
5. Position head in “sniffing” position or maintain spinal motion restriction, if indicated.
6. Hold the KING LT(S)-D with the dominant hand
7. Open the mouth and apply chin-lift with the non-dominant hand
8. Introduce the KING LT(S)-D into corner of mouth at 90° angle
9. As the tube tip passes under the tongue, rotate the tube back to midline

gentle downward pressure

continuous ETCO2 monitoring. A normal four-phase waveform should be visible if
ventilating appropriately
15. If ventilation is not accomplished, without deflating the cuff, pull back slightly and reattempt ventilations. If pulling back slightly does not seat the device properly, then
deflate the cuff, slowly withdraw the tube and re-assess
16. Ventilate with oxygen at the appropriate rate (monitor for chest rise/fall, SpO2 and ETCO2)
17. If the KING LT(S)-D is removed, suction MUST be available.

Procedure:
1. Formally announce the procedure will be performed and brief all team members
a. Move the patient as able to optimize operator position, lighting, and safety
b. Monitor ECG, SpO2, respiratory rate, NIBP, and capnography
2. Perform a kit dump and set up equipment in a stable secure area
a. Open packaging just enough to facilitate access but maintain sterility and cleanliness

left shoulder
c. Aspirate during needle advancement and monitor for fluid return
d. If no fluid is aspirated, withdraw the needle and redirect it systematically changing
posterior trajectory and left to right angles
e. Withdraw the needle if ST elevation injury pattern or ventricular ectopy occurs
indicating epicardial contact
f. Stop needle advancement when blood or fluid is present and advance catheter fully,
aspirate as much as possible
6. After initial aspiration, remove the needle leaving the catheter in place with a three-way
stopcock attached for future aspiration
a. Secure the catheter with tape

• Use the ETT cuff manometer to check cuff pressures
o Adult target: 20 – 25 cmH2O
o Pediatric target: 15 – 20 cmH2O
• Consider placing a c-collar to help maintain tube placement, especially on pediatric
patients
• Place the patient on a ventilator for transport, regardless of estimated transport time
• Maintain sedation for patient comfort as well as crew and aircraft safety. See Pain
Management and Sedation guidelines

paralysis for patients with a history of combativeness or agitation. Consider the
constraints of the aircraft/vehicle, patient size, and crew safety. For other patients,
consider using sedation only without ongoing paralysis

o Repeat q 30 min or more frequently PRN

rocuronium 1 mg/kg IV or 1.8mg/kg IM

finalizing the clinical chart
o Do not document the procedure was “successful” without documenting the name

8.31 Spinal Motion Restriction
• Indications
Suspected spinal injury
Contraindications
• None
BLS
Equipment:
1. Cervical collar
2. Webbing or quick-release belts (duct tape is discouraged)
3. Scoop (preferred) or backboard, and/or stretcher
4. Head securing method
Procedure:
1. Perform spinal motion restriction (SMR) assessment. If ANY of the following are present,
apply SMR:
a. Altered mental status
b. Evidence of intoxication
c. Midline neck and/or back pain and/or tenderness
d. Focal neurologic deficits or symptoms
e. Anatomic deformity of the spine
f. Distracting injury or circumstance, including extreme agitation or emotional
distress
g. Torticollis in children (may require immobilization in position found)
h. A communication barrier that prevents accurate assessment
i. Increased suspicion of spinal injury by provider (mechanism of injury, age, etc.)
2. If SMR is indicated:
a. Patient is reliable and ambulatory on-scene or can safely self-extricate:
i. Place cervical collar on patient. Direct patient to limit spine movement
ii. Allow the patient to move him or herself to the unloaded stretcher
iii. Secure the patient to the stretcher
iv. Transport the patient in a supine position or position of comfort
v. Upon arrival at the hospital, assist the patient in moving to the hospital’s
stretcher. If any pain experienced, use a slide board to maintain spinal
alignment.
3. If the patient has altered mental status, intoxication, a distracting injury or circumstance,
a communication barrier, is unreliable, requires extrication, or is not ambulatory:
a. Place cervical collar on patient. Direct patient to limit spine movement
b. Use a scoop or backboard as needed to move patient to the stretcher
c. Remove backboard or scoop once the patient is on the stretcher, maintaining inline spinal alignment. Secure the patient to the stretcher. The patient may remain
on the backboard or scoop if moving would otherwise delay critical
interventions/rapid transport
d. Transport the patient in a supine position
e. Upon arrival at the hospital, move the patient to the hospital stretcher while
maintaining inline spinal alignment with a slide board

Restriction
1. Consider extremes of age and the cognitive ability of the patient to understand
assessment question
2. Patients ≥65 years old are more prone to skeletal injury with even minimal traumatic

3. Patients must clearly understand the language spoken AND must have the cognitive
ability to comprehend the answers asked in the SMR assessment
4. Immobilized patients are at high risk for aspiration secondary to nausea/vomiting or

10. It is acceptable to use the hard backboard if the patient is already immobilized and flight

11. If utilized, placement on the hard backboard should be performed as late as possible
and the backboard should be padded with a blanket or Back-Raft whenever possible

Equipment:

Prepare
1. Place the patient in a supine position with support under the shoulders and neck in midhyperextension, unless a c-spine injury is suspected
2. Don face/eye protection
a. Air and blood are often forcibly expelled when the cricothyroid membrane is

Palpate / Identify
4. Palpate the neck in the midline and locate the slight depression just below the inferior
border of the thyroid cartilage and just above the cricoid cartilage.
a. This is the cricothyroid membrane.
b. Approximate location is three to four finger breadths (patient’s fingers) above the
sternal notch.
c. IF you are UNABLE to IDENTIFY the cricothyroid membrane, make a 2” vertical
incision over the suspected location, then dissect until you are able to
palpate/locate the membrane.
Stabilize

a. STABILIZE the airway by stretching skin across the thyroid cartilage or by
maintaining grasp on the thyroid cartilage with your non-dominate hand.
b. Best practice is to use your thumb and long finger to allow palpation of the site
with your index finger.
c. Make a small, pinpoint incision over the site with the top of the scalpel.
6. Puncture the membrane with the Ruiz hook, then hook along the inferior edge of the
thyroid cartilage and lift toward the head.

ALS
4. Set Mode
a. Use the arrow keys to navigate to Mode, press the Select button, and then use the
arrow keys and the Select button to set the Pacer Mode to Demand
5. Set Rate
a. Use the arrow keys to navigate to Rate, press the Select button, and then use the
arrow keys and the Select button to set the Pacer Rate to a value 10-20 ppm
higher than the patient’s intrinsic heart rate. If no intrinsic rate exists, use 80 ppm.
b. You can increase or decrease the pacer rate by a value of 5 ppm for rates below
100, and by 10 ppm for rates above 100.
6. Turn on Pacer
a. Use the arrow keys to navigate to Start Pacer, then press the Select button to
select it. The Pacing window (below) displays behind the Pacer Settings window.
7. Set Pacer Output (mA)
a. In the Pacer Settings window, use the arrow keys and the Select button to adjust
the pacer output
b. Typical threshold ranges from 40 – 80 mA
c. The pacer output is adjustable in 10 mA increments when increasing the output,
and in 5 mA increments when decreasing the output.
d. Observe the ECG for evidence of electrical capture.
e. Select the lowest output current that achieves both electrical and mechanical
capture.
f. If the Pacer Settings window disappears before you have set the output current,
press the PACER button again to display the settings window
8. Determine Capture
a. It is important to recognize when pacing stimulation has produced a ventricular
response (capture).
b. Determination of capture must be assessed both electrically and mechanically in
order to ensure appropriate circulatory support of the patient.
i. Electrical capture is determined by the presence of a widened QRS
complex, the loss of any underlying intrinsic rhythm, and the appearance
of an extended, and sometimes enlarged, T-wave. Ventricular response is
normally characterized by suppression of the intrinsic QRS complex.
ii. Mechanical capture is assessed by palpation of the peripheral pulse. To
avoid mistaking muscular response to pacing stimuli for arterial
pulsations, use ONLY the following locations for palpating pulse during
pacing:
a. Femoral artery
b. Right brachial or radial artery
9. Changing ECG leads and size can sometimes be helpful in determining capture
a. The shape and size of the paced ECG waveforms can vary depending on the ECG
lead configuration chosen; variation from patient to patient can be expected.

10. Determine Optimal Threshold
a. The ideal pacer current is the lowest value that maintains capture — it is usually
about 10% above threshold.
b. Location of the hands-free or therapy electrodes affects the current required to
obtain ventricular capture.
c. Typically, the lowest threshold is obtained when the position of the electrodes
provides the most direct current pathway through the heart while avoiding large
chest muscles.
d. Lower stimulation currents produce less skeletal muscle contraction and are

9.01 Death In The Field
• Do Not Resuscitate
o If any of the following are present:
▪ A pulseless, apneic patient in a mass casualty incident (MCI) or multiple patient
scene where the resources of the system are required for the stabilization of living
patients
▪ Decapitation
▪ Rigor mortis in a warm environment
▪ Decomposition
▪ Skin discoloration in dependent body parts (dependent lividity)
▪ Pulseless and apneic with a valid Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order
▪ Idaho, Oregon, Montana, or Washington POLST (Physician Orders for Life Sustaining
Treatment)
▪ Signed DNR order from another state
o Special Considerations:
▪ Most victims of electrocution, lightning, and drowning should have resuscitative
efforts initiated and be transported to an appropriate hospital
o Notes:
▪ Crews may transport a patient who would normally have resuscitation terminated at
the scene if deemed appropriate for safety or compassion issues (e.g., gang related
violence, pediatrics, etc.)
▪ Oregon patients: If an original POLST cannot be produced, contact the POLST
Registry at (877) 367-7657.
• Upon confirmation of patient identity, the Registry can relay Section A and B
POLST orders. Registry staff do not interpret orders
▪ Hospital DNR orders are not valid outside of the hospital
▪ Death of Pre-Established Hospice Patients:
▪ If the patient dies during transport, the crew may continue to their home or hospice
facility and place them into the bed or location of the family’s choice.
▪ The family will notify the hospice facility (if the decedent is taken to a home) to take
care of notifying the ME and other details.
• POLST orders and decision making
o In the pulseless and apneic patient who does not meet DEATH IN THE FIELD criteria but is
suspected to be a candidate for withholding resuscitation, begin CPR and contact OLMC
o A patient with decision-making capacity or the legally authorized representative has the
right to direct his or her own medical care and can change or rescind previous directives
o EMS providers may honor a POLST Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR) order signed by a
physician, naturopathic physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant
o DNAR orders apply only to the patient in cardiopulmonary arrest and do not indicate the
types of treatment that a person not in arrest should receive. POLST was developed to
convey orders in other circumstances
o Remember DNR does not mean do not treat

Death In
The Field
• Once Death is Determined
o Treat the recently dead with respect
o Tell family and friends of the death honestly. Use the words “death” or “dead.” Avoid using
euphemisms such as “passed away” or “gone”
o Avoid using past tense terms when speaking to survivors of the recently dead
o Allow family and friends to express their emotions
▪ Listen to them if they want to talk but don’t push them
o Give factual information
o Genuine warmth and compassion will be more helpful than almost anything else for
survivors
▪ Don’t feel it necessary to say the “right” things. Listening often provides grieving
people with the most comfort
• Focusing on Survivors
o See to it that survivors have a support system present before you leave.
▪ Consider calling friends, family, clergy, or neighbors to be with them.
▪ Respect the survivors’ wishes to be alone.
o Explain the next steps to them after you have pronounced death.
▪ This will include the police coming to make reports, possibly the medical examiner,
and the possible need for an autopsy
o Before moving or altering the body, contact the Medical Examiner’s office as soon as
possible
o Allow family and friends to say their good-byes if possible
o Help survivors make decisions such as which people should be called. If they ask you to
make calls, try to comply.
▪ Mention the need to find a funeral home if one has not been chosen
o Clergy may also be helpful with this decision
• Death of a Child
o Do not be overly silent, which may imply guilt to the parents
o Ask the parents only necessary questions and do not judge or evaluate them
▪ Do not tell them what they “should have” been doing before your arrival
o Remind parents to arrange for childcare of other children, if applicable
o Listen carefully to their statements and answer with accurate information
o Successful management of child deaths requires supportive, compassionate, and tactful
measure

9.02 Destination Determination
1. Patient destination on scene calls should be determined utilizing several factors:
a) Statewide Destination protocols
b) Patient preference
c) Direction by local EMS providers or protocols, and/or via Online Medical Control
d) In the absence of these factors, patients should generally be transported to the closest
appropriate facility based upon the patient’s illness and condition
2. Level I and II trauma facilities both provide definitive care for severely injured patients, with Level I
facilities also providing trauma education and research
3. In cases where transport destinations are not addressed in Statewide Protocols or these
Guidelines, and transport time to the hospital offering definitive care exceeds the closest hospital
by >30 minutes, strongly consider contacting the closest facility for advice regarding the
appropriate destination
4. Unstable patients may benefit from stabilization at the closest facility before transferring to the
facility offering definitive care
5. The presence of an extremity tourniquet is significant to trauma leveling.
a) If the patient has a tourniquet, please include this as part of your pre arrival report to
ensure proper trauma team response
6. When a patient and/or family member requests transport to a facility that deviates from local
protocols or these Guidelines:
a) Assess medical decision-making capacity. See Refusal of Treatment.
b) A patient with decision-making capacity or their family may request a destination facility of
their choosing, but they must be provided enough information regarding the risks and
benefits to make an informed decision
c) If the patient requests a facility more than 25 NM beyond the closest appropriate facility,
advise them we will honor the request, but their insurance may not cover the additional
cost. We want them to make an informed decision
7. If, in your opinion, the patient makes a less-than-optimal choice after weighing the information

transfer is appropriate

Washington Stroke Triage Destination Procedure
The purpose of the Prehospital Stroke Triage and Destination Procedure is to identify stroke patients in
the field and take them to the most appropriate hospital, which might not be the nearest hospital.
Stroke treatment is time-critical – the sooner patients are treated, the better their chances of survival
and recovering function.
For strokes caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain (ischemic, the majority of strokes), clotbusting medication (tPA) must be administered within 4.5 hours from the time the patient was last known
well, a treatment that can be given at WA DOH Level 1, 2 or 3 stroke centers (for a list of categorized
hospitals, please click here).
If a patient presents to EMS with a severe stroke, they are more likely to have blockage of a large
vessel and can benefit from mechanical clot retrieval (thrombectomy). Thrombectomy must begin by 24
hours since last known well, and is a more complex intervention, only available in Level I and a
small number of Level II stroke centers.
There are 3 key elements to determine the appropriate destination hospital:
1. FAST stroke screen to identify a patient with a high probability of stroke
2. Stroke Severity Score to determine if a patient meets criteria for “severe” stroke
3. Time since Last Known Well (LKW) which helps determine eligibility for tPA and thrombectomy
STEPS to determine destination:
1. Do a FAST Stroke Screen Assessment: (facial droop, arm drift, speech changes, time since (LKW)
is a simple way to tell if someone might be having a stroke.
a. If FAST is negative, stroke is less likely, and standard destination procedures apply.
b. If FAST is positive (face or arms or speech is abnormal), it’s likely the patient is having a
stroke, and the EMS provider moves on to assessing stroke severity
2. Assess severity: The stroke severity assessment scores the FAST stroke screen. Patients get
points for deficits:
a. Facial droop:
i. 1 point if present
ii. 0 points if absent
b. Arm drift (have patient hold arms up in air):
i. 2 points if an arm falls rapidly
ii. 1 point if slowly drifts down
iii. 0 points if the arms stay steady
c. Grip strength:
i. 2 points if no real effort can be made
ii. 1 point if grip is clearly there but weak
iii. 0 points if grips seem of full strength
d. Add up the points: A score > 4 is interpreted as “severe”

Destination
Determination
3. Determine time since LKW: It is important to use the LKW time as opposed to when symptoms
were first noticed.
a. If a patient woke up in the morning with symptoms and was well when they went to bed,
time LKW is the time they went to bed
b. If stroke symptoms occur when the patient is awake, LKW could be the same time the
symptoms started if the patient or a bystander noticed the onset
c. LKW time could also be prior to symptoms starting if a patient delays reporting
d. symptoms or, for example, someone discovers a patient with symptoms but saw them well
2 hours prior
4. Determine Destination:
a. Time since LKW < 6 hours and “Severe” (score > 4):
i. This group benefits from preferential transport to a thrombectomy stroke center
ii. The patient should be taken directly to the nearest thrombectomy stroke center
provided it is no more than 15 extra minutes travel compared to the nearest stroke
center.
b. Time since LKW is > 24 hours (regardless of severity score):
i. These patients should be taken to nearest Level I or II stroke center provided it is no
more than 15 minutes greater than to a nearer Level III stroke center.
c. Time since LKW 6-24 hours but NOT “Severe”:
i. These patients should be taken directly to the nearest Level I or Level II stroke
center provided it is no more than 15 extra minutes travel compared to a nearer
Level 3 stroke center
d. Time since LKW 6-24 hours AND “Severe”:
i. Transport to nearest Level I or II Stroke Center with endovascular capability
provided transport time is no more than 30-60 min greater than to a nearer Level II
or Level III Stroke Center.
e. Regional care procedures and county operating procedures may provide additional
guidance
5. Notification: Immediately notify the destination hospital of incoming stroke.
a. If the patient is within 6 hours LKW, call a stroke alert according to county operating
procedures or locally determine protocol
6. Document: key medical history, medication list and next of kin phone contacts; time on scene;
FAST assessment and results (or reason why not); blood glucose level; LKW time (including
unknown); and whether the hospital was notified from the field and if it was a stroke alert

Purpose
Washington Trauma Triage:
The National Guideline for Field Triage of Injured Patients was developed by a
multidisciplinary panel led by the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma. The
guideline has been adopted by the Department of Health (DOH) based on the recommendation of
the State Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Trauma Steering Committee in association with
the Prehospital and Hospital Technical Advisory Committees.
The guideline represents the current best practice for the triage of trauma patients and
allows EMS providers to quickly and accurately determine if the casualty is a major or moderate
trauma patient. It also aids in decision making to determine the most appropriate transfer facility
location.
The triage procedure is described below in Figure 1. It consolidates triage criteria into two
main categories based on risk of serious injury: High-Risk Criteria (red box) includes Injury
Patterns, Mental Status, and Vital Signs. Moderate-Risk Criteria (yellow box) includes
Mechanism of Injury and EMS Judgment. Each risk category is aligned with recommendations for
a destination trauma service. Figure 1. is intended to be read from top to bottom, left to right.
Any certified EMS provider can identify a major trauma patient and alert receiving
hospitals. Hospitals will activate their trauma team based on their internal policies and
procedures. EMS providers should follow regional Patient Care Procedures (PCPs) and County
Operating Procedures (COPs) for engaging other system partners such as air ambulance and
advanced level ground ambulance services to coordinate the most appropriate and expedient
transport modality for a trauma patient.
Red Criteria / High Risk for Serious Injury
Assess Injury Patterns, Mental Status & Vital Signs
Assessment of injury patterns, mental status, and vital signs meeting red criteria should
require alerting and rapidly transporting to the closest level I or II trauma service within 30
minutes transport time. If the transport time is greater than 30 minutes, transfer should be to the
nearest most appropriate trauma service.
If unable to maintain a patent airway, consider rendezvous with an Advanced Life Support
(ALS) unit or transporting to the nearest facility capable of definitive airway management. The
presence of specific injury patterns with normal vital signs, lack of pain, or normal levels of
consciousness; requires calling medical control and alerting the receiving hospital. Pediatric
patients meeting the red criteria should be preferentially triaged to designated pediatric trauma
service.
Yellow Criteria / Moderate Risk for Serious Injury
Assess Mechanism of Injury and EMS Judgement
An assessment of the mechanism of injury meeting yellow criteria should require alerting
and rapidly transporting to the closest appropriate trauma service within 30 minutes (air or
ground). The destination trauma service need not be the highest-level trauma service. Risk factors
coupled with "provider judgment" are reasons for the provider to contact Medical Control and
discuss appropriate destinations for these patients.
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE

Destination
Determination
In some cases, the decision may be to transport to the nearest trauma service or a
resource hospital. Patients with combined burns and trauma should be preferentially transported
to a trauma center with burn care capability. Pediatric patients should be preferentially
transported to a designated pediatric trauma service.
PCPs and local COPs provide additional details about the appropriate hospital destination.
They are intended to further define how the system operates. The Prehospital Trauma Triage
Destination Procedure and PCPs work in "hand in glove" fashion to address trauma patient care
needs.

9.03 Physician On Scene
1. In all cases, when a physician on scene offers to provide assistance and/or medical direction, Life
Flight Network personnel will determine the physician’s identity and medical specialty
a. A physician on scene may not provide assistance and/or medical direction unless the
following conditions are met:
2. The physician must be currently licensed to practice medicine in the state where the scene is
located
a. The physician’s medical specialty must be pertinent to the patient’s medical condition
b. The physician agrees to accompany the patient to the hospital (subject to pilot approval for
fixed wing or rotor transports) and understands they are responsible for any and all care
given
c. The physician agrees to sign a copy of the LFN Patient Care Record as soon as possible
(see #6, below)
d. When possible, contact OLMC or the Life Flight Network Medical Director to speak with the
on-scene physician regarding their offer of assistance or care
3. The following physicians are exempt from this policy provided they are licensed to practice
medicine in the state in which the call occurs:
a. Life Flight Network Medical Directors
b. The patient’s attending physician
4. At no time will Life Flight Network personnel render care outside their scope of practice and
training at the direction of a physician on scene, including those listed in number 3 above
5. If during transport, the patient’s condition should warrant treatment other than that requested by
the attending physician, on-line medical control or a Life Flight Network Medical Director must be
contacted for advice and concurrence
6. Because of the nature of our electronic charting process, an event log entry must be completed to
fully document the circumstances of an on-scene physician assuming patient control. This event
log will contain at a minimum:
a. The physician’s name
b. Address
c. Phone number
d. License number
e. Specialty
f. All orders carried out at the direction of the physician
g. A statement indicating the physician was physically present during all times once they
assumed control, including:
i. Accompanying the patient to the receiving hospital, and
ii. That the physician verbally agreed to sign a copy of the electronic chart as soon as
practical
7. The electronic chart containing the original signature of the physician will be maintained at the
Life Flight Network administrative offices for a period not less than 25 years
8. Upon completion of a transport of this nature, immediately notify the Life Flight Network Medical
Director and the Clinical Manager On Call (CMOC)
9. A Quality Management (QM) report will be completed any time a physician assumes or attempts
to assume medical control

9.04 Refusal of Treatment/Transport
1. Our goal is to transport and appropriately treat all individuals who require our service
a. This goal notwithstanding, we will encounter individuals who will refuse a particular
treatment, air transport, or our services altogether
2. Assess and document medical decision-making capacity
a. Patients with reasonable medical decision-making capacity may refuse care if they
understand the consequences
3. Patient-initiated refusals of care must be documented in the patient care record
a. LFN 201.07 “Refusal of Treatment Form, Addendum A” will be used to document any
incident when a patient refuses a treatment recommended by the clinical crew, refuses air
transport, or refuses transport altogether
4. Findings that suggest reasonable medical decision-making capacity include:
a. Normal or near-normal vital signs
b. Normal level of consciousness
c. Normal orientation or orientation at usual baseline
d. Absence or minimal use of intoxicants
e. Coherent, non-pressured speech
f. Appropriate insight
g. Understanding of the risks of refusal
i. The patient needs to be able to reiterate these risks when asked
5. The following types of patients may not refuse care and should be transported to the closest
appropriate facility:
a. Intentional overdose
b. Attempted or threatened suicide
c. Grossly intoxicated
d. Minor*
e. Inadequate medical decision-making capacity
f. For aviation safety reasons, consider sedation or RSI when the patient cannot refuse care
and is agitated or combative
6. “Patients are allowed to make poor choices”
a. Nonetheless, Life Flight Network personnel may, in their role as patient advocate and in
certain patient-specific situations, elect to speak with the patient’s family and/or friends to
enlist their help in convincing the patient to accept medical care
i. The patient’s privacy and HIPAA rights must be protected during this conversation.
7. Whenever possible, it is preferable to have the individual who is refusing transport altogether
speak directly with a physician via on-line medical control
8. *The following minors are considered emancipated (state dependent) and may refuse treatment
and sign the refusal of treatment form:
a. Oregon: patients under 18 years of age are considered emancipated if they are:
i. Married, or
ii. Emancipated by court order
b. Washington: patients under 18 years of age are considered emancipated if they are:
i. Married to a person aged 18 or older, or
ii. Emancipated by court order

9.06 Termination of Resuscitation During Transport
Termination of Resuscitation CANNOT be performed without an advanced airway in place and
waveform ETCO2
1. The following must be present in order to consider termination of resuscitation in medical arrest
patients without contacting OLMC.
a. An advanced airway in place AND confirmed with waveform ETCO2
b. Age ≥ 18 years
c. Not knowingly pregnant
d. Patent vascular access
e. No neurological responses present
f. No ROSC obtained at any point in resuscitation
g. No identified reversible causes present
h. ECG remains in asystole or agonal after 20 minutes of resuscitation that follows the
appropriate AHA and LFN guidelines
i. Verification of absent heart tones for at least 60 seconds
2. Resuscitation during transport should not be terminated if the transport time to the original
destination hospital or airport is < 15 minutes
a. To better permit evaluation of patient status to include pulses, heart sounds, and airway
status, all efforts should be made to transport the patient to a receiving hospital or
destination airport and unloaded from the aircraft before decision to terminate
resuscitation
b. If the transport time to the original destination hospital is > 15 min, resuscitation may be
terminated in patients in cardiopulmonary arrest who meet criteria per Death in the Field
with OLMC consult
c. If unable to contact OLMC and termination of resuscitation is within your state scope of
practice, you may terminate resuscitation, otherwise you should continue the transport.
i. Note GPS coordinate of aircraft at time resuscitation was terminated
d. ETCO2 and ECG strips showing the rhythm at time of termination in two different leads
must be obtained and uploaded to the PCR
3. The Clinical Manager on Call (CMOC) and the LFN Communications Center will be notified when
resuscitation efforts are terminated inside a LFN transport vehicle
4. The Communications Center will alert the appropriate Medical Examiner or Coroner as soon as
they are made aware resuscitation efforts have been terminated
a. Rotor Wing Aircraft:
i. Notify receiving facility of termination of efforts
ii. Continue transport to receiving facility
iii. If remainder of transport is expected to be >30 min, contact the CMOC for
guidance.
iv. The body should be left in the aircraft until the appropriate Medical Examiner or
Coroner can retrieve the body

i. Proceed to the destination airport
ii. The body will be left inside the aircraft until the appropriate Medical Examiner or

advise there was a death in the vehicle
ii. The Medical Examiner or Coroner will determine the appropriate rendezvous

10.06b EMS VAN Tool
• Arm Drift:
o If there is no arm drift, the patient is considered VAN negative, and no further testing is
done
o If the arm drift is positive, proceed to VAN testing
• Vision:
o With the patient looking at your nose, test vision in all 4 quadrants by holding up your
hand sequentially in each quadrant (right upper, right lower, left upper, left lower).
o Ask the patient to count how many fingers you are holding up (vary number in each
quadrant)
o Have the patient track your finger with their eyes, moving it left to right then right to left
and ask if they have double vision
o Failure to count fingers correctly or presence of double vision is considered positive
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE

Stroke Scales
• Aphasia:
o Have the patient name two objects (e.g., point to watch, hold up a pen, hold up your
phone).
o Have them repeat a statement (already done under Speech in the FAST exam). Have the
patient follow two commands: “close your eyes” and “make a fist”
o Failure to identify the two objects, repeat a statement or follow both commands is
considered positive
Neglect:
o Look at patient’s eyes for forced gaze, looking persistently to right or left
o Then with patient’s eyes closed, touch their right arm, then left arm, then both arms.
o With each touch, have patient identify which arm you are touching
o The presence of forced gaze or inability to identify which arm is being touched is
considered positive
Scoring VAN
o No arm weakness = VAN negative
o Arm weakness, but VAN tests all normal or negative = VAN negative
o Arm weakness and any one VAN test positive = VAN positive
